title: Osho on Fear, Death and the Present Moment
description: What Osho taught about fear and death, in plain words. Every fear is, underneath, the fear of death. A mother who searched the whole town for a mustard seed, a tea master facing a samurai's sword, the burning ghats by the river, a servant who ran from Death to the next city, and a man hanging from a vine who found a strawberry. Then a meditation on the breath that is happening now.

chapters.title: Osho on Fear, Death and the Present Moment

beats.say: Look closely at any fear. Fear of losing your job, fear of being alone, fear of what people will say. Go deep enough into it... and underneath, you will find one fear.
The fear of death. Of not being. All the small fears are its children. Osho spoke about death again and again.
We don't talk about it. We hide the dead quickly, we change the subject, we say: not now, not me, not yet. But it is the one thing that is certain.
His advice was: "Let there be a let-go." So tonight, let us not run. Let us sit with the old stories, and look at death straight in the face.
A young mother named Kisa Gotami lost her only child. A small boy, hardly able to walk. She could not accept it. She carried the little body from house to house, begging: give me medicine for my son.
People turned away. Some cried with her. Then an old man said: go to the Buddha. He is staying outside the town. Perhaps he has a medicine.
She ran to the Buddha and fell at his feet. And the Buddha said: Yes, I will help you. Bring me a handful of mustard seeds.
But the seeds must come from a house where nobody has ever died. Not a father, not a mother, not a child, not a servant.
She was so happy. Mustard seeds! Every house has mustard seeds. She ran to the first door. Yes, of course, take them. But has anyone died in this house? Oh yes... my grandmother, last winter.
The second house. My husband. The third house. My brother, in the river. House after house, all day long. Everywhere there were seeds. Nowhere was there a house without death.
By evening she sat down outside the town. And slowly she understood. Death is not my enemy alone. It comes to every house. It is the way of things.
She buried her son with her own hands. Then she went back to the Buddha, and never left him again. Osho taught that this seeing is the end of fear.
Small children are afraid of the dark. Why? Not because something is there. Because they cannot see. The unknown frightens them.
We are the same. Death is the great unknown. Nobody has come back from the other side with a full report. So the mind imagines the worst.
But the strange thing is this. You are also afraid of life. Of really living. Of loving totally, of dancing totally, of saying yes totally.
A man who has not lived is very much afraid of dying. Because he has not yet tasted anything. He wants more time, more time.
And a man who has lived each moment fully is not so worried. He has eaten the meal. He can get up from the table with a smile.
Osho taught: the medicine for the fear of death is not a belief. It is life. Live so totally that nothing is left over.

chapters.title: The Tea Master and the Samurai

beats.say: In old Japan there was a tea master who served a great lord. One day, in the city, he bumped into a rough samurai, who took it as an insult and challenged him to a duel.
The tea master had never held a sword in his life. He knew he would die the next morning. So he went to the best sword master in the city and said: teach me at least how to die well.
The sword master said: first, serve me a cup of tea. So the tea master did what he had done every day of his life, slowly, carefully, with his whole being.
When he finished, the sword master said: there, you need nothing more. Tomorrow, face him the way you served this tea. Raise the sword, close your eyes, and be totally present.
In the morning the tea master stood in front of the angry samurai. He raised the sword above his head, calm, still, without one trace of fear. He was not waiting for death. He was simply there.
The samurai looked at him for a long time. He could find no gap, no weakness, no fear to cut into. Finally he lowered his sword, bowed, and walked away.
Osho taught that fear lives in the future. In what might happen. The man who is totally in the present has nowhere for the fear to stand.
If you go to Benares, go to the burning ghats by the river. The fires burn there day and night. Body after body, wrapped in cloth, is carried down to the water.
And just a few steps away, people are bathing, children are flying kites, someone is selling tea. Life and death, sitting side by side.
Sit there for one evening and watch. Something strange happens. Your own death begins to look less like a stranger, and more like an old neighbour.
The fire takes the body. The body was borrowed from the earth, and now it is given back. But who was living in it?
That is the question the river has been asking for thousands of years. Osho's answer: find, while you are alive, the one who does not burn.

chapters.title: The Servant Who Ran from Death

beats.say: In Baghdad, a rich merchant sent his servant to the market. The servant came running back, white as a sheet, trembling all over.
Master, he cried, in the market I saw Death. She looked at me and made a strange sign. Please, lend me your fastest horse. I will ride to Samarra tonight, where she will never find me.
The merchant gave him the horse, and the servant galloped away. Then the merchant himself went down to the market, and there he saw Death, standing in the crowd.
Why did you frighten my servant this morning? he asked. And Death said: I did not mean to frighten him. I was only surprised to see him here in Baghdad.
You see, I have an appointment with him tonight... in Samarra.
We all run. To Samarra, to the next job, the next city, the next pleasure. But the running only takes us faster to the place we are running from.
Osho taught: stop running. Turn around. Look at what you are afraid of. Most of the time, there is nothing there but your own shadow.
A man was walking across a field, and a tiger saw him. He ran, and the tiger came after him. He came to the edge of a cliff and jumped over, catching hold of a wild vine.
There he hung. Above him, the tiger was waiting. And when he looked down, far below, another tiger was looking up at him, licking its lips.
Then two little mice, one white and one black, began to nibble at the vine. Slowly, slowly, the vine was getting thinner.
And just then he saw, growing out of the rock beside him, one wild strawberry. Red and ripe. Holding the vine with one hand, he picked it with the other.
How sweet it tasted!
The tiger above is the past. The tiger below is the future. The mice are day and night. And the strawberry, Osho taught, is this moment. Eat it... it is sweet.
Now let us sit, and watch the breath, the way Osho taught Vipassana. Close your eyes. Feel the breath coming in through the nose. Cool. And going out. Warm.
This breath is not in the past. It is not in the future. It is only happening now. Every breath is a doorway into the present.
Notice the small pause at the end of the out-breath. The breath goes out... and for a moment, nothing. Then it comes back by itself.
Every out-breath is a small death. Every in-breath is a small birth. You have been dying and being born, again and again, all your life.
Rest in the pause. Don't be afraid of it. In the pause, there is great peace.
If a fear comes, let it come. Watch it like a visitor. It will sit for a while, and then it will leave, because you are not feeding it.
Only this breath. Only this moment. Nothing else exists.
And now take one deep breath, the deepest of the day. Open your eyes slowly. Welcome back to this precious, passing moment.
